claim: Leukemia stem cells (LSCs) are regarded as the origins and key therapeutic targets of leukemia.
source: Leukemia stem cells (LSCs) are regarded as the origins and key therapeutic targets of leukemia, but limited knowledge is available on the key determinants of LSC 'stemness'.
evidence: This is a general statement about the field's understanding of LSCs, representing established scientific consensus.

claim: SPI1 is a master regulator whose LSC-specific expression determines the molecular signature and activity of LSCs in the murine Pten-null T-ALL model.
source: Using single-cell RNA-seq analysis, we identify a master regulator, SPI1, the LSC-specific expression of which determines the molecular signature and activity of LSCs in the murine Pten-null T-ALL model.
evidence: This claim is supported by single-cell RNA-seq analysis performed in the study.

claim: Spi1 expression and LSC 'stemness' are maintained by a β-catenin-SPI1-HAVCR2 regulatory circuit independent of the leukemogenic driver mutation.
source: Although initiated by PTEN-controlled β-catenin activation, Spi1 expression and LSC 'stemness' are maintained by a β-catenin-SPI1-HAVCR2 regulatory circuit independent of the leukemogenic driver mutation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing the regulatory circuit functions independently of PTEN loss.

claim: Perturbing any component of the β-catenin-SPI1-HAVCR2 circuit either genetically or pharmacologically can prevent LSC formation or eliminate existing LSCs.
source: Perturbing any component of this circuit either genetically or pharmacologically can prevent LSC formation or eliminate existing LSCs.
evidence: This claim is supported by genetic and pharmacological experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: LSCs lose their 'stemness' when Spi1 expression is silenced by DNA methylation.
source: LSCs lose their 'stemness' when Spi1 expression is silenced by DNA methylation, but Spi1 expression can be reactivated by 5-AZ treatment.
evidence: This claim is supported by DNA methylation analysis and functional studies.

claim: Spi1 expression can be reactivated by 5-AZ treatment.
source: LSCs lose their 'stemness' when Spi1 expression is silenced by DNA methylation, but Spi1 expression can be reactivated by 5-AZ treatment.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing 5-AZ treatment effects.

claim: Similar regulatory mechanisms may be present in human T-ALL.
source: Importantly, similar regulatory mechanisms may be also present in human T-ALL.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on observations in human T-ALL cell lines and datasets.

claim: Current treatment for T-ALL includes high-intensity combination chemotherapies.
source: Current treatment for T-ALL includes high-intensity combination chemotherapies.
evidence: This represents established clinical knowledge about T-ALL treatment.

claim: Up to 20% of pediatric and 40% of adult T-ALL patients relapse.
source: However, such treatment may cause short- and long-term side effects, and up to 20% of pediatric and 40% of adult T-ALL patients relapse (Atak et al., 2013; Girardi et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Leukemia stem cells are considered to be one of the main causes of drug resistance and therapeutic relapse.
source: Leukemia stem cells (LSCs) are considered to be one of the main causes of drug resistance and therapeutic relapse (Batlle and Clevers, 2017; Blackburn et al., 2014; Chiu et al., 2010; Visvader, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: LSCs can self-renew and differentiate into leukemic blast cells.
source: Like hematopoietic stem cells, LSCs can self-renew and differentiate into leukemic blast cells (Bonnet and Dick, 1997; Reya et al., 2001), which makes them ideal candidates for high-efficiency and low-toxicity targeted therapies.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to foundational literature on LSCs.

claim: In the Pten-null T-ALL model, LSCs are enriched in the Lin-CD3+KITmid cell subpopulation.
source: In this model, LSCs are enriched in the Lin-CD3+KITmid cell subpopulation; these cells are self-renewable and responsible for T-ALL initiation and drug resistance (Guo et al., 2008; Guo et al., 2011; Schubbert et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work on the Pten-null T-ALL model.

claim: Both LSC-enriched and leukemic blast subpopulations share similar genetic alterations, including Pten loss and Tcra/d-Myc translocation.
source: However, since both LSC-enriched and leukemic blast subpopulations share similar genetic alterations, including Pten loss and Tcra/d-Myc translocation (Guo et al., 2008), these driver mutations are unlikely to determine LSC 'stemness'.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work and leads to an inference about LSC stemness.

claim: Treating the Pten-null T-ALL model with PI3K inhibitors is effective only before the onset of leukemia, not after leukemia is already underway.
source: Furthermore, treating the Pten-null T-ALL model with PI3K inhibitors is effective only before the onset of leukemia, not after leukemia is already underway (Guo et al., 2011; Schubbert et al., 2014), suggesting that this driver mutation is not responsible for the maintenance of LSC 'stemness' once it has been generated.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous experimental work.

claim: The previously identified Lin-CD3+KITmid LSC-enriched subpopulation contains heterogeneous cells, of which 30% are MYC low, rapamycin- and JQ1-resistant, and relatively quiescent in terms of cell cycle.
source: We reported previously that the LSC-enriched Lin-CD3+KITmid subpopulation in the Pten-null T-ALL model contains heterogeneous cells, of which 30% are MYC low, rapamycin- and JQ1 (a BRD4 inhibitor)-resistant, and relatively quiescent in terms of cell cycle (Guo et al., 2008; Schubbert et al., 2014) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work and reference to a figure.

claim: WGCNA identified one module with a LSChigh-Blast0 expression pattern containing 220 genes.
source: We isolated LSC-enriched and blast subpopulations for RNA-seq analysis (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, upper panel) and identified one module with a LSChigh-Blast0 expression pattern by Weighted Gene Co-expression Network Analysis (WGCNA) (Zhang and Horvath, 2005) (Figure 1A, yellow module).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data analysis and reference to figures.

claim: Approximately 45% of the genes in the yellow module encode membrane proteins such as Havcr2 and Itgax.
source: Approximately, 45% of the genes in this module encode membrane proteins such as Havcr2 (HAVCR2) and Itgax (ITGAX) (Figure 1B–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene ontology analysis shown in the figures.

claim: The cell surface expression of HAVCR2 and ITGAX are highly correlated.
source: The cell surface expression of HAVCR2 and ITGAX, as measured by FACS analysis, are highly correlated and can further separate the previously identified Lin-CD3+KITmid LSC-enriched subpopulation into several subgroups (Figure 1D, upper panel), among which the HAVCR2high or HAVCR2high ITGAXhigh subgroups are most abundant in the thymus, the critical organ for T cell development and T-ALL initiation (Guo et al., 2008;Guo et al., 2011) (Figure 1D, lower panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by FACS analysis data shown in the figure.

claim: The HAVCR2high or HAVCR2high ITGAXhigh subgroups are most abundant in the thymus.
source: The cell surface expression of HAVCR2 and ITGAX, as measured by FACS analysis, are highly correlated and can further separate the previously identified Lin-CD3+KITmid LSC-enriched subpopulation into several subgroups (Figure 1D, upper panel), among which the HAVCR2high or HAVCR2high ITGAXhigh subgroups are most abundant in the thymus, the critical organ for T cell development and T-ALL initiation (Guo et al., 2008;Guo et al., 2011) (Figure 1D, lower panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative FACS data shown in the figure.

claim: Single-cell RNA-seq analysis identified four subgroups.
source: To determine whether these heterogeneous groups are organized hierarchically from LSCs to blasts during T-ALL development, we conducted single-cell RNA-seq analysis and identified four subgroups (Figure 1E; Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, lower panel; Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by single-cell RNA-seq data and PCA analysis shown in the figures.

claim: Pseudotime analysis indicates that LSCs follow a continuous developmental path towards blasts, progressing from HAVCR2high through HAVCR2mid and HAVCR2low to blasts.
source: Pseudotime analysis (Trapnell et al., 2014) further indicates that LSCs follow a continuous developmental path towards blasts, progressing from HAVCR2high through HAVCR2mid and HAVCR2low to blasts (Figure 1F), which can also be visualized by pseudotime analysis of Havcr2 and Itgax expression (Figure 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by pseudotime analysis of single-cell RNA-seq data shown in the figures.

claim: The HAVCR2high subgroup is enriched in the hematopoietic stem cell/late progenitor pathways and is relatively quiescent.
source: Single-cell transcriptome analysis indicates that the HAVCR2high subgroup is enriched in the hematopoietic stem cell/late progenitor pathways and is relatively quiescent, while the blast subpopulation is enriched in Myc lymphoma pathways and active in the cell cycle (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by GSEA analysis and cell cycle analysis shown in the figure.

claim: The blast subpopulation is enriched in Myc lymphoma pathways and active in the cell cycle.
source: Single-cell transcriptome analysis indicates that the HAVCR2high subgroup is enriched in the hematopoietic stem cell/late progenitor pathways and is relatively quiescent, while the blast subpopulation is enriched in Myc lymphoma pathways and active in the cell cycle (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by GSEA analysis and cell cycle analysis shown in the figure.

claim: The HAVCR2high subgroup has the lowest c-MYC level among the four subgroups.
source: Consistent with this observation, the HAVCR2high subgroup also has the lowest c-MYC level among the four subgroups (Figure 2B), suggesting that the HAVCR2high subgroup may contain the MYClow cells within the previously defined Lin-CD3+KITmid LSC-enriched subpopulation (Guo et al., 2008; Schubbert et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by intracellular FACS analysis of MYC levels shown in the figure.

claim: Nearly every Lin-CD3+KITmidHAVCR2high cell is capable of inducing T-ALL development.
source: Cells from the HAVCR2high subgroup have the highest leukemia-initiating capacity—nearly every Lin-CD3+KITmidHAVCR2high cell is capable of inducing T-ALL development, compared to 1/14 of the cells in the Lin-CD3+KITmid subgroup and 1/28 of the cells in the Lin-CD3+KITmidHAVCR2low subgroup (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by limiting dilution transplantation assay data shown in the figure.

claim: 1/14 of the cells in the Lin-CD3+KITmid subgroup are capable of inducing T-ALL development.
source: Cells from the HAVCR2high subgroup have the highest leukemia-initiating capacity—nearly every Lin-CD3+KITmidHAVCR2high cell is capable of inducing T-ALL development, compared to 1/14 of the cells in the Lin-CD3+KITmid subgroup and 1/28 of the cells in the Lin-CD3+KITmidHAVCR2low subgroup (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by limiting dilution transplantation assay data shown in the figure.

claim: 1/28 of the cells in the Lin-CD3+KITmidHAVCR2low subgroup are capable of inducing T-ALL development.
source: Cells from the HAVCR2high subgroup have the highest leukemia-initiating capacity—nearly every Lin-CD3+KITmidHAVCR2high cell is capable of inducing T-ALL development, compared to 1/14 of the cells in the Lin-CD3+KITmid subgroup and 1/28 of the cells in the Lin-CD3+KITmidHAVCR2low subgroup (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by limiting dilution transplantation assay data shown in the figure.

claim: Cells from the HAVCR2high subgroup can induce T-ALL lethality much earlier than cells from the other two subgroups.
source: Consistent with these findings, cells from the HAVCR2high subgroup can also induce T-ALL lethality much earlier than cells from the other two subgroups (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by survival curve data shown in the figure.

claim: HAVCR2 is a novel surface marker for the isolation of pure LSCs.
source: Thus, HAVCR2 is a novel surface marker for the isolation of pure LSCs, and the HAVCR2high subgroup represents the true LSC population in the Pten-null T-ALL model (Table 1).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the limiting dilution and transplantation data.

claim: The HAVCR2high subgroup represents the true LSC population in the Pten-null T-ALL model.
source: Thus, HAVCR2 is a novel surface marker for the isolation of pure LSCs, and the HAVCR2high subgroup represents the true LSC population in the Pten-null T-ALL model (Table 1).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the limiting dilution and transplantation data.

claim: Approximately 70% of the HAVCR2high LSC signature genes overlap with SPI1 target genes identified during T cell development.
source: Importantly, approximately 70% of the HAVCR2high LSC signature genes overlap with SPI1 target genes identified during T cell development (Zhang et al., 2012)(Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison with published SPI1 target genes and shown in the figure.

claim: Spi1 expression is highest in the HAVCR2high subgroup, which is opposite to the differential expression of Myc.
source: The pseudotemporal ordering of the single-cell RNA-seq data and the FACS analyses demonstrate that Spi1 expression is highest in the HAVCR2high subgroup, which is opposite to the differential expression of Myc (Figure 4B–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by pseudotime analysis and FACS data shown in the figures.

claim: SPI1 binds strongly to Havcr2 promoter region 2.
source: SPI1 binds strongly to Havcr2 promoter region 2 (Zhu et al., 2015) (Figure 4D) and the Tcra enhancer (EA) region in the translocated Tcra/d-Myc allele (Figure 4E), as well as to the E2 region of the WT allele (Shi et al., 2013)(Figure 4F), suggesting that it may have regulatory effects on both genes.
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in the figure.

claim: SPI1 binds to the Tcra enhancer (EA) region in the translocated Tcra/d-Myc allele.
source: SPI1 binds strongly to Havcr2 promoter region 2 (Zhu et al., 2015) (Figure 4D) and the Tcra enhancer (EA) region in the translocated Tcra/d-Myc allele (Figure 4E), as well as to the E2 region of the WT allele (Shi et al., 2013)(Figure 4F), suggesting that it may have regulatory effects on both genes.
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in the figure.

claim: SPI1 binds to the E2 region of the WT Myc allele.
source: SPI1 binds strongly to Havcr2 promoter region 2 (Zhu et al., 2015) (Figure 4D) and the Tcra enhancer (EA) region in the translocated Tcra/d-Myc allele (Figure 4E), as well as to the E2 region of the WT allele (Shi et al., 2013)(Figure 4F), suggesting that it may have regulatory effects on both genes.
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in the figure and citation.

claim: The overexpression of Spi1 in T-ALL blast cells significantly increases the expression of Havcr2 and other known SPI1 target genes, such as Itgax and Lmo2.
source: The overexpression of Spi1 in T-ALL blast cells significantly increases the expression of Havcr2 and other known SPI1 target genes, such as Itgax and Lmo2 (Champhekar et al., 2015; Turkistany and DeKoter, 2011; Yashiro et al., 2017), but downregulates Myc mRNA and protein levels (Figure 4G–H).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR and Western blot data shown in the figures.

claim: The overexpression of Spi1 in T-ALL blast cells downregulates Myc mRNA and protein levels.
source: The overexpression of Spi1 in T-ALL blast cells significantly increases the expression of Havcr2 and other known SPI1 target genes, such as Itgax and Lmo2 (Champhekar et al., 2015; Turkistany and DeKoter, 2011; Yashiro et al., 2017), but downregulates Myc mRNA and protein levels (Figure 4G–H).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR and Western blot data shown in the figures.

claim: SPI1 knockdown in a human T-ALL cell line downregulates the expression of SPI1 target genes but upregulates MYC expression.
source: In contrast, SPI1 knockdown in a human T-ALL cell line downregulates the expression of SPI1 target genes but upregulates MYC expression (Figure 4I).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data from knockdown experiments shown in the figure.

claim: The positive correlation between SPI1 and the expression of HAVCR2 as well as that of SPI1 target genes such as ITGAX and LMO2 can be found in human T-ALL datasets.
source: Importantly, the positive correlation between SPI1 and the expression of HAVCR2 as well as that of SPI1 target genes such as ITGAX and LMO2 can be found in human T-ALL datasets (Liu et al., 2017; Van Vlierberghe et al., 2011)(Figure 5), suggesting that the regulation of HAVCR2 expression by SPI1 could play an important role in human T-ALLs.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of published human T-ALL datasets shown in the figure.

claim: The lethality caused by T-ALL is delayed proportionally to the numbers of Spi1 allele that are deleted.
source: Kaplan-Meier survival analysis shows that the lethality caused by T-ALL is delayed proportionally to the numbers of Spi1 allele that are deleted (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by survival curve data from genetic deletion experiments shown in the figure.

claim: No infiltrating leukemia cells can be detected in the liver of the Pten/Spi1 double knockout mice.
source: The tissue architectures of the thymus and spleen appear normal, and no infiltrating leukemia cells can be detected in the liver of the mutant mice (dKO) (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by histological analysis shown in the figure.

claim: HAVCR2high LSCs and CD3+ blasts are absent in the thymus, spleen and bone marrow of the Pten/Spi1 double knockout mice.
source: FACS analyses also show the absence of HAVCR2high LSCs and CD3+ blasts in the thymus, spleen and bone marrow (BM) of the dKO mice (Figure 6C–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by FACS analysis data shown in the figures.

claim: Spi1 deletion can restore spleen weight and organ morphology.
source: Spi1 deletion can also restore spleen weight and organ morphology (Figure 6B; Figure 6E).
evidence: This claim is supported by spleen weight measurements and histological analysis shown in the figures.

claim: PI3K activation can rescue the T cell developmental block in Spi1-null T cell progenitors.
source: These results suggest that PI3K activation can rescue the T cell developmental block in Spi1-null T cell progenitors (Champhekar et al., 2015; Spain et al., 1999), similar to the findings in our previous report on Pten;Rag-null mice (Guo et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is inferred from FACS-Gal analysis and supported by citations.

claim: SPI1 is essential for Pten-null LSC 'stemness' and T-ALL development.
source: Therefore, SPI1 is essential for Pten-null LSC 'stemness' and T-ALL development.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the genetic deletion experiments showing loss of LSCs and T-ALL upon Spi1 deletion.

claim: During T cell development, Spi1, with other T progenitor cell factors and growth factor receptors such as Bcl11a, Lmo2, Flt3 and Kit, is highly expressed at the early T progenitor (ETP) and double-negative 1 (DN1) stage and is then immediately downregulated during T cell commitment.
source: During T cell development, Spi1, with other T progenitor cell factors and growth factor receptors such as Bcl11a, Lmo2, Flt3 and Kit, is highly expressed at the early T progenitor (ETP) and double-negative 1 (DN1) stage and is then immediately downregulated during T cell commitment (Zhang et al., 2012) (Figure 7A, upper panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published work and shown in the figure.

claim: The expression patterns of Spi1 and these factors and receptors are largely unchanged in the Pten-null T-ALL model compared to normal T cell development.
source: Interestingly, our pseudotemporal ordering of the single-cell RNA-seq data indicates that the expression patterns of Spi1 and these factors and receptors are largely unchanged in the Pten-null T-ALL model compared to normal T cell development (Figure 7A, lower panels).
evidence: This claim is supported by pseudotime analysis of single-cell RNA-seq data shown in the figure.

claim: Spi1-GFP expression is significantly upregulated at the ETP/DN1 stage in Pten-null T-ALL model mice.
source: Indeed, when we crossed Spi1-GFP reporter mice (Nutt et al., 2005) to Pten-null T-ALL model mice, we found that Spi1-GFP expression is significantly upregulated at the ETP/DN1 stage (Figure 7B).
evidence: This claim is supported by FACS analysis of Spi1-GFP reporter mice shown in the figure.

claim: β-Catenin is an important transcription factor regulating Spi1 expression in the T cell lineage.
source: β-Catenin is an important transcription factor regulating Spi1 expression in the T cell lineage (Rosenbauer et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published work.

claim: β-catenin is critical for LSC self-renewal.
source: Previous works by us and others suggest that β−catenin is critical for LSC self-renewal (Guo et al., 2008) and RAG-dependent aberrant TCR rearrangement (Dose et al., 2014; Guo et al., 2011), a mechanism underlying the reoccurring Tcra/d -Myc translocation caused by PTEN loss or β−catenin activation observed in T-ALLs (Guo et al., 2008 Kaveri et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The overexpression of β-catenin in a human T-ALL cell line leads to the significantly increased expression of SPI1 from its endogenous promoter.
source: Indeed, the overexpression of β-catenin in a human T-ALL cell line leads to the significantly increased expression of SPI1 from its endogenous promoter and subsequently promotes the expression of its target gene HAVCR2 but downregulates MYC expression (Figure 8A).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data from overexpression experiments shown in the figure.

claim: The overexpression of β-catenin in a human T-ALL cell line promotes the expression of HAVCR2 but downregulates MYC expression.
source: Indeed, the overexpression of β-catenin in a human T-ALL cell line leads to the significantly increased expression of SPI1 from its endogenous promoter and subsequently promotes the expression of its target gene HAVCR2 but downregulates MYC expression (Figure 8A).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data from overexpression experiments shown in the figure.

claim: PTEN loss or PI3K/AKT activation activates β-catenin by phosphorylating GSK-3β and preventing GSK-3β-mediated β-catenin degradation.
source: PTEN loss or PI3K/AKT activation is known to activate β−catenin by phosphorylating GSK-3β and preventing GSK-3β-mediated β−catenin degradation (Dan et al., 2008; Kikushige et al., 2015; Persad et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published work describing this mechanism.

claim: The HAVCR2high, HAVCR2low and blast subgroups have similar levels of P-GSK-3β due to PTEN loss.
source: Although the HAVCR2high, HAVCR2low and blast subgroups have similar levels of P-GSK-3β due to PTEN loss (Figure 8B, upper and lower panels), the HAVCR2high subgroup has a much higher level of non-phospho-β−catenin (the active form of β−catenin) and SPI1 than HAVCR2low and blast subgroups in vivo (Figure 8C and E, upper and lower panels), suggesting that SPI1-mediated LSC formation may depend on mechanisms other than the oncogenic driver mutation PTEN loss.
evidence: This claim is supported by intracellular FACS analysis shown in the figure.

claim: The HAVCR2high subgroup has a much higher level of non-phospho-β-catenin (the active form of β-catenin) and SPI1 than HAVCR2low and blast subgroups in vivo.
source: Although the HAVCR2high, HAVCR2low and blast subgroups have similar levels of P-GSK-3β due to PTEN loss (Figure 8B, upper and lower panels), the HAVCR2high subgroup has a much higher level of non-phospho-β−catenin (the active form of β−catenin) and SPI1 than HAVCR2low and blast subgroups in vivo (Figure 8C and E, upper and lower panels), suggesting that SPI1-mediated LSC formation may depend on mechanisms other than the oncogenic driver mutation PTEN loss.
evidence: This claim is supported by intracellular FACS analysis shown in the figure.

claim: HAVCR2 signaling can activate NFκB and β-catenin and promote AML LSC formation and self-renewal.
source: HAVCR2 signaling can activate NFκB and β−catenin and promote AML LSC formation and self-renewal (Kikushige et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published work on AML.

claim: The HAVCR2high subgroup has the highest level of both phospho-p65 and non-phospho-β-catenin among the four subgroups.
source: Intracellular FACS analyses show that among the four subgroups, the HAVCR2high subgroup, which has the highest Spi1 expression, also has the highest level of both phospho-p65 and non-phospho-β−catenin (Figure 8D–E, upper and lower panels), indicating that HAVCR2 signaling must play an important role in the hyperactivation of NFκB and β−catenin.
evidence: This claim is supported by intracellular FACS analysis shown in the figures.

claim: The genetic deletion of Spi1 can prevent both HAVCR2high LSC formation at the ETP/DN1 stage and T-ALL development.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, the genetic deletion of Spi1 can prevent both HAVCR2high LSC formation at the ETP/DN1 stage and T-ALL development (Figure 8F).
evidence: This claim is supported by FACS analysis of Spi1 deletion mice shown in the figure.

claim: The pharmacological inhibition of β-catenin activation by the novel tankyrase inhibitor BAY6060 can significantly reduce the number of HAVCR2high LSCs in vivo in late-stage T-ALL.
source: The pharmacological inhibition of β−catenin activation by the novel tankyrase inhibitor BAY6060, but not the inhibition of PI3K activity by BAY1082439 alone (Hill et al., 2017), can also significantly reduce the number of HAVCR2high LSCs in vivo in late-stage T-ALL (Figure 8G).
evidence: This claim is supported by FACS analysis of drug-treated mice shown in the figure.

claim: The inhibition of PI3K activity by BAY1082439 alone cannot significantly reduce the number of HAVCR2high LSCs in vivo in late-stage T-ALL.
source: The pharmacological inhibition of β−catenin activation by the novel tankyrase inhibitor BAY6060, but not the inhibition of PI3K activity by BAY1082439 alone (Hill et al., 2017), can also significantly reduce the number of HAVCR2high LSCs in vivo in late-stage T-ALL (Figure 8G).
evidence: This claim is supported by FACS analysis of drug-treated mice shown in the figure.

claim: The Spi1 promoter is significantly hypomethylated in LSCs compared to blasts and normal T cell controls.
source: Although the global methylation patterns across the LSC signature and blast signature genes are similar (Figure 9A–B), the Spi1 promoter is significantly hypomethylated in LSCs compared to blasts and normal T cell controls (Figure 9C).
evidence: This claim is supported by RRBS analysis shown in the figures.

claim: The 4 CpG islands on the Spi1 promoter are not methylated in the HAVCR2high subgroup but gradually become methylated in the HAVCR2mid and HAVCR2low subgroups and are completely methylated in blasts.
source: Consistently, the 4 CpG islands on the Spi1 promoter (Fernández-Nestosa et al., 2013) are not methylated in the HAVCR2high subgroup but gradually become methylated in the HAVCR2mid and HAVCR2low subgroups and are completely methylated in blasts (Figure 9D), which may explain the trend in Spi1 expression and Spi1-controlled Havcr2 and Itgax expression (Figure 4B, upper panel; Figure 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by bisulfite sequencing data shown in the figure.

claim: Treating leukemic blasts with the DNMT inhibitor 5-AZ can increase the expression of Spi1 and its regulated LSC signature genes in vitro.
source: Conversely, treating leukemic blasts with the DNMT inhibitor 5-AZ can increase the expression of Spi1 and its regulated LSC signature genes in vitro (Figure 9E) and induces the SPI1+ and MYClow subgroups in vivo (Figure 9F), demonstrating that Spi1 expression is reversibly regulated by DNA methylation, which in turn regulates LSC signature gene expression.
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data from 5-AZ treatment experiments shown in the figure.

claim: 5-AZ treatment induces the SPI1+ and MYClow subgroups in vivo.
source: Conversely, treating leukemic blasts with the DNMT inhibitor 5-AZ can increase the expression of Spi1 and its regulated LSC signature genes in vitro (Figure 9E) and induces the SPI1+ and MYClow subgroups in vivo (Figure 9F), demonstrating that Spi1 expression is reversibly regulated by DNA methylation, which in turn regulates LSC signature gene expression.
evidence: This claim is supported by FACS analysis of 5-AZ treated mice shown in the figure.

claim: Spi1 expression is reversibly regulated by DNA methylation.
source: Conversely, treating leukemic blasts with the DNMT inhibitor 5-AZ can increase the expression of Spi1 and its regulated LSC signature genes in vitro (Figure 9E) and induces the SPI1+ and MYClow subgroups in vivo (Figure 9F), demonstrating that Spi1 expression is reversibly regulated by DNA methylation, which in turn regulates LSC signature gene expression.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the 5-AZ treatment experiments showing reactivation of Spi1 expression.

claim: KE-37 expresses SPI1 and HAVCR2, while CEM does not.
source: KE-37 expresses SPI1 and HAVCR2, while CEM does not (Figure 10A), consistent with the methylation status of the SPI1 promoter (Figure 10B).
evidence: This claim is supported by FACS analysis of human T-ALL cell lines shown in the figure.

claim: The expression of SPI1 and HAVCR2 in KE-37 and CEM is consistent with the methylation status of the SPI1 promoter.
source: KE-37 expresses SPI1 and HAVCR2, while CEM does not (Figure 10A), consistent with the methylation status of the SPI1 promoter (Figure 10B).
evidence: This claim is supported by FACS analysis and bisulfite sequencing data shown in the figures.

claim: 5-AZ treatment can upregulate the expression of SPI1 and its target HAVCR2 but downregulate c-MYC expression in CEM cells.
source: 5-AZ treatment can upregulate the expression of SPI1 and its target HAVCR2 but downregulate c-MYC expression in CEM cells, similar to the effects of our blast treatment, while no change can be detected in KE-37 cells (Figure 10C), demonstrating that SPI1 expression is also regulated by DNA methylation in human T-ALL.
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data from 5-AZ treatment of human T-ALL cell lines shown in the figure.

claim: No change in SPI1, HAVCR2, or MYC expression can be detected in KE-37 cells after 5-AZ treatment.
source: 5-AZ treatment can upregulate the expression of SPI1 and its target HAVCR2 but downregulate c-MYC expression in CEM cells, similar to the effects of our blast treatment, while no change can be detected in KE-37 cells (Figure 10C), demonstrating that SPI1 expression is also regulated by DNA methylation in human T-ALL.
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data from 5-AZ treatment of human T-ALL cell lines shown in the figure.

claim: SPI1 expression is regulated by DNA methylation in human T-ALL.
source: 5-AZ treatment can upregulate the expression of SPI1 and its target HAVCR2 but downregulate c-MYC expression in CEM cells, similar to the effects of our blast treatment, while no change can be detected in KE-37 cells (Figure 10C), demonstrating that SPI1 expression is also regulated by DNA methylation in human T-ALL.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the 5-AZ treatment experiments in human T-ALL cell lines.

claim: 5-AZ treatment significantly accelerated T-ALL development induced by CEM cells in vivo.
source: 5-AZ treatment significantly accelerated T-ALL development (Figure 10D).
evidence: This claim is supported by survival curve data from transplantation experiments shown in the figure.

claim: DB1976 can significantly inhibit the expression of Havcr2 and other SPI1 target genes in vitro.
source: DB1976 can significantly inhibit the expression of Havcr2 and other SPI1 target genes in vitro (Figure 11A) and reduce the number of HAVCR2high LSCs in vivo (Figure 11B, left panel), confirming that SPI1 is not only important for LSC formation but also for LSC maintenance.
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data from DB1976 treatment experiments shown in the figure.

claim: DB1976 can reduce the number of HAVCR2high LSCs in vivo.
source: DB1976 can significantly inhibit the expression of Havcr2 and other SPI1 target genes in vitro (Figure 11A) and reduce the number of HAVCR2high LSCs in vivo (Figure 11B, left panel), confirming that SPI1 is not only important for LSC formation but also for LSC maintenance.
evidence: This claim is supported by FACS analysis of DB1976-treated mice shown in the figure.

claim: SPI1 is important for both LSC formation and LSC maintenance.
source: DB1976 can significantly inhibit the expression of Havcr2 and other SPI1 target genes in vitro (Figure 11A) and reduce the number of HAVCR2high LSCs in vivo (Figure 11B, left panel), confirming that SPI1 is not only important for LSC formation but also for LSC maintenance.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the DB1976 treatment experiments showing effects on existing LSCs.

claim: Only when combined with rapamycin could DB1976 significantly reduce the leukemia burden.
source: However, only when combined with a debulking anti-PI3K agent such as rapamycin (Guo et al., 2008) could DB1976 significantly reduce the leukemia burden, as demonstrated by the nearly complete absence of leukemic blasts in the hematopoietic organs (Figure 11B, right panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by FACS analysis of combination treatment shown in the figure.

claim: Combination treatment with DB1976 and rapamycin can markedly prolong the animal lifespan.
source: Consequently, combination treatment can markedly prolong the animal lifespan (Figure 11C), restore the spleen weight and morphology, and eliminate infiltrating leukemic cells in the lung, kidney and liver without a significant change in animal body weight (Figure 11D–E; Figure 11—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by survival curve data shown in the figure.

claim: Combination treatment with DB1976 and rapamycin can restore the spleen weight and morphology.
source: Consequently, combination treatment can markedly prolong the animal lifespan (Figure 11C), restore the spleen weight and morphology, and eliminate infiltrating leukemic cells in the lung, kidney and liver without a significant change in animal body weight (Figure 11D–E; Figure 11—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by spleen weight measurements and histological analysis shown in the figures.

claim: Combination treatment with DB1976 and rapamycin can eliminate infiltrating leukemic cells in the lung, kidney and liver without a significant change in animal body weight.
source: Consequently, combination treatment can markedly prolong the animal lifespan (Figure 11C), restore the spleen weight and morphology, and eliminate infiltrating leukemic cells in the lung, kidney and liver without a significant change in animal body weight (Figure 11D–E; Figure 11—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by histological analysis and body weight measurements shown in the figures.

claim: The inhibition of tankyrase by BAY6060 can significantly reduce β-catenin activity and consequently decrease Spi1 expression and the number of HAVCR2high LSCs in vivo.
source: The inhibition of tankyrase by BAY6060 can significantly reduce β-catenin activity and consequently decrease Spi1 expression and the number of HAVCR2high LSCs in vivo (Figure 12A).
evidence: This claim is supported by FACS analysis of BAY6060-treated mice shown in the figure.

claim: BAY6060 and BAY1082439 in combination could significantly prolong the animal lifespan and almost completely eliminate LSCs and blasts.
source: In combination, BAY6060 and BAY1082439 could significantly prolong the animal lifespan and almost completely eliminate LSCs and blasts (Figure 12B, Figure 11E and Figure 8G).
evidence: This claim is supported by survival curve data and FACS analysis shown in the figures.

claim: HAVCR2 is normally not expressed in hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells.
source: Compared with β-catenin and SPI1, HAVCR2 may be a better therapeutic target as it is normally not expressed in hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (Kikushige et al., 2010), and inhibition of HAVCR2 would therefore be less toxic.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published work.

claim: An anti-HAVCR2 antibody has been used clinically in immunotherapy and in targeting AML LSCs.
source: An anti-HAVCR2 antibody has been used clinically in immunotherapy and in targeting AML LSCs (Kikushige et al., 2010; Koyama et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published work.

claim: When combined with rapamycin, the anti-HAVCR2 antibody showed a therapeutic effect similar to that seen for DB1976/rapamycin and BAY6060/BAY1082439 combinations.
source: When combined with rapamycin, the anti-HAVCR2 antibody showed a therapeutic effect similar to that seen for DB1976/rapamycin and BAY6060/BAY1082439 combinations (Figure 11D–E and Figure 12C; Figure 11—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by survival curve data and histological analysis shown in the figures.

claim: Inhibiting any component in the β-catenin-SPI1-HAVCR2 regulatory circuit will inhibit LSC 'stemness' maintenance and lead to the effective elimination of HAVCR2-positive T-ALL cells in the presence of an effective debulking agent targeting the PI3K pathway.
source: Together, these results suggest that inhibiting any component in the β-catenin-SPI1-HAVCR2 regulatory circuit will inhibit LSC 'stemness' maintenance and lead to the effective elimination of HAVCR2-positive T-ALL cells in the presence of an effective debulking agent targeting the PI3K pathway, such as rapamycin or BAY1082439.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combination treatment experiments with different inhibitors.

claim: Two layers of control mechanisms play essential roles in leukemogenesis.
source: Our study suggests that two layers of control mechanisms may play essential roles in leukemogenesis (Figure 13).
evidence: This is a summary statement inferred from all the experimental data in the study.

claim: The first layer is driven by the loss of the PTEN tumor suppressor or the activation of the PI3K pathway, which leads to β-catenin activation, Tcra/d-Myc translocation and T-ALL development.
source: The first layer is driven by the loss of the PTEN tumor suppressor or the activation of the PI3K pathway, which leads to β-catenin activation, Tcra/d-Myc translocation and T-ALL development.
evidence: This claim summarizes the first layer of control based on the study's findings and previous work.

claim: The second layer is controlled by the master regulator SPI1, which determines LSC signature gene expression and maintains LSC 'stemness'.
source: The second layer is controlled by the master regulator SPI1, which determines LSC signature gene expression and maintains LSC 'stemness' (Figures 4–6).
evidence: This claim summarizes the second layer of control based on the study's findings.

claim: SPI1 upregulation is initiated by PI3K-controlled β-catenin activation, while the LSC-specific expression of SPI1 is reinforced by the β-catenin-SPI1-HAVCR2 regulatory circuit.
source: SPI1 upregulation is initiated by PI3K-controlled β-catenin activation,while the LSC-specific expression of SPI1 is reinforced by the β-catenin-SPI1-HAVCR2 regulatory circuit (Figure 8).
evidence: This claim summarizes the mechanism of SPI1 regulation based on the study's findings.

claim: Once formed, LSCs are very sensitive to any perturbation of the β-catenin-SPI1-HAVCR2 regulatory circuit but are less dependent on the PI3K pathway.
source: Once formed, LSCs are very sensitive to any perturbation of this regulatory circuit but are less dependent on the PI3K pathway, as inhibiting the PI3K pathway at the leukemia stage has little effect on the LSC number (Figures 11–12)(Guo et al., 2008; Blackburn et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by the drug treatment experiments and citations.

claim: SPI1 is silenced by DNA methylation, which leads to the downregulated expression of LSC signature genes, the loss of LSC 'stemness' and leukemic differentiation.
source: SPI1 is silenced by DNA methylation, which leads to the downregulated expression of LSC signature genes, the loss of LSC 'stemness' and leukemic differentiation (Figures 9–10).
evidence: This claim summarizes the mechanism of LSC differentiation based on the study's findings.

claim: The PTEN loss and Tcra/d-Myc translocation are hardwired and present in both LSCs and leukemia blasts.
source: Although the PTEN loss and Tcra/d-Myc translocation in the first layer of the leukemogenesis mechanism are hardwired and present in both LSCs and leukemia blasts, the SPI1 expression and maintenance in the second layer of the LSC 'stemness' mechanism is reversible and present only in LSCs (Figure 13).
evidence: This claim contrasts the two layers of control mechanisms based on the study's findings.

claim: The SPI1 expression and maintenance in the second layer of the LSC 'stemness' mechanism is reversible and present only in LSCs.
source: Although the PTEN loss and Tcra/d-Myc translocation in the first layer of the leukemogenesis mechanism are hardwired and present in both LSCs and leukemia blasts, the SPI1 expression and maintenance in the second layer of the LSC 'stemness' mechanism is reversible and present only in LSCs (Figure 13).
evidence: This claim contrasts the two layers of control mechanisms based on the study's findings.

claim: Similar two-layer control mechanisms may also be present in other types of cancer in which CSCs are known to play essential roles.
source: Similar two-layer control mechanisms may also be present in other types of cancer in which CSCs are known to play essential roles.
evidence: This is a speculative statement extending the findings to other cancers.

claim: Targeting driver mutations or dysregulated pathways in the first layer may be sufficient for debulking the leukemia mass but not for eliminating LSCs unless the mechanism for maintaining LSC 'stemness' is simultaneously inhibited.
source: First, targeting driver mutations or dysregulated pathways in the first layer may be sufficient for debulking the leukemia mass but not for eliminating LSCs unless the mechanism for maintaining LSC 'stemness' is simultaneously inhibited (Figures 11–12).
evidence: This claim represents a therapeutic implication inferred from the combination treatment experiments.

claim: The reactivation of SPI1 expression could be a potential mechanism for LSC-mediated therapeutic resistance.
source: Second, since the expression of the LSC master regulator SPI1 can be reversibly regulated by epigenetic mechanisms (Figures 9–10), this model would predict poorer outcomes if leukemia controlled by such a mechanism was treated with 5-AZ or similar agents and would suggest that the reactivation of SPI1 expression could be a potential mechanism for LSC-mediated therapeutic resistance.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about therapeutic implications based on the reversibility of SPI1 expression.

claim: PTEN and the PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway controlled by PTEN are critical for the etiology of human T-ALL.
source: PTEN and the PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway controlled by PTEN are critical for the etiology of human T-ALL (Gutierrez et al., 2009; Larson Gedman et al., 2009; Liu et al., 2017; Maser et al., 2007; Palomero et al., 2007), and our study may illuminate the understanding and treatment of T-ALLs associated with PTEN loss or PI3K activation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published work on human T-ALL.

claim: SPI1 expression is upregulated by β-catenin and silenced by DNA methylation in human T-ALL cell lines.
source: We demonstrate that SPI1 expression is upregulated by β-catenin and silenced by DNA methylation in human T-ALL cell lines, similar to the findings in the Pten-null T-ALL model (Figures 9–10).
evidence: This claim is supported by experiments in human T-ALL cell lines shown in the figures.

claim: SPI1 controls the expression of HAVCR2 and other LSC signature genes in human T-ALL cell lines and clinical samples.
source: SPI1 also controls the expression of HAVCR2 and other LSC signature genes in human T-ALL cell lines and clinical samples (Figure 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by experiments in human T-ALL cell lines and analysis of clinical samples shown in the figure.

claim: HAVCR2high LSCs can be detected in the peripheral blood of leukemic mice.
source: As HAVCR2high LSCs can be detected in the peripheral blood of leukemic mice (our unpublished data), further investigation is worthwhile to explore the potential use of this approach as a noninvasive strategy for stratifying T-ALL and monitoring the treatment response.
evidence: This claim is based on unpublished data mentioned in the manuscript.
